summary:
This run covered 7 evals; 2 were negative-trigger evals (negative-training-pending, negative-live-fault-is-it-aws) that were skipped by design (should_trigger: false) — both variants correctly did not fire, but no further comparison data exists for them. One eval (endpoint-slow-and-erroring) had every assertion marked "inconclusive" and expected_output at 0/1 for both variants, with quality comparison skipped — this eval essentially produced no usable signal for either variant, suggesting a measurement/setup issue rather than a performance gap.

For the four remaining substantive evals:

- idle-endpoint-wasting-money: Both variants met expected output (1/1, medium confidence) and tied on assertion pass rate (4/6). Of the six assertions, three always passed for both (no differentiation) and one always failed for both (LLM-SM check-id citation — a gap in both variants). Two assertions split: with_skill correctly distinguished "no datapoints" from a measured zero while without_skill did not; conversely without_skill avoided exposing a raw account ID while with_skill did not. A single quality-pair comparison favored without_skill (on actionability specifically), with medium confidence. Runtime/cost were similar (with_skill 42s/$0.36 vs without_skill 47s/$0.40).

- serverless-cold-start-provisioned-concurrency: expected_output diverged — with_skill met it (1/1, medium confidence) while without_skill did not (0/1). Assertion pass rates tied at 3/6 overall, but with different patterns: without_skill correctly explained cold-start-as-expected-behavior (with_skill did not), while with_skill correctly cited an LLM-SM check-id (without_skill did not). Two assertions always failed for both (distinguishing no-datapoints from measured zero, and giving remediation strictly as an operator command). Quality comparison was skipped for this eval. Variant_b ran notably faster and cheaper (20s/$0.17) than with_skill (43s/$0.36).

- serverless-async-silent-failures: Both variants failed to meet expected output (0/1, high confidence) and both scored low on assertions (1/6), with four of six assertions always failing for both variants — pointing to a shared gap in checking AsyncInferenceConfig/notification setup, backlog scaling policy, and no-datapoints handling, rather than a difference between variants. The one assertion both passed was not exposing raw account IDs. Quality comparison was skipped. Variant_a ran faster/cheaper (1m20s/$0.67) than without_skill (1m39s/$0.83).

- batch-transform-partial-output: Both variants failed to meet expected output (0/1). Variant_a had a notably higher assertion pass rate (3/5, 60%) than without_skill (1/5, 20%), driven by two assertions where with_skill passed and without_skill failed (citing a batch check-id, and giving remediation as a command with a batch check-id). One assertion always failed for both (reconciling output count vs input count — the core intended check), and one always failed for both (account ID exposure). Quality comparison was skipped. Variant_b ran faster/cheaper (24s/$0.20) than with_skill (46s/$0.39).

Overall pattern: across the evaluable cases, neither variant consistently outperforms the other — each has evals and specific assertions where it does better, and several assertions/evals where both fail or both pass identically, indicating shared gaps in the underlying behavior (e.g., LLM-SM check-id citation, no-datapoints handling, backlog/notification checks) rather than a one-sided variant weakness. Where one variant is faster/cheaper, it sometimes also has a lower assertion or expected-output pass rate (e.g., serverless-cold-start), and sometimes not (e.g., batch-transform, where the faster variant also failed more assertions) — so speed/cost advantages do not map cleanly onto quality. Output-consistency data was not available (null) for any eval, and most quality-pair comparisons were skipped, so confidence in a quality-based read is limited. Several expected-output judgments carried only medium confidence, which should temper how strongly the expected-output pass/fail differences are read.

Output consistency across repeated runs is not available (null) for both variants.

Overall: this eval appears to have failed to execute meaningfully — the trigger didn't fire, no assertions resolved, and no quality pairs were evaluated. There is no reliable basis here to describe a difference, tradeoff, or similarity between with_skill and without_skill; the data is essentially absent rather than indicating parity or divergence.

idle-endpoint-wasting-money.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task (one trial/pair) around diagnosing a SageMaker endpoint using CloudWatch metrics, auto-scaling configuration, and account-exposure concerns. Given the very small sample size (1 run), all findings should be read as a single data point rather than a robust trend.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior under test fired as expected, and both without_skill and with_skill fully met the expected output (1/1, 100%), though the confidence backing that expected-output judgment was only "medium" for both, so this agreement is not a strong signal.

Assertions (6 total per variant, same pass rate 4/6 = 67% for both): Looking behind the tied aggregate, the per-assertion detail shows a mixed and informative picture:
- Three assertions passed for both variants (checking CurrentInstanceCount/Invocations instead of relying on InService status; correctly treating an empty scalable-targets result as fixed capacity; recommending remediation as an operator command rather than calling a mutating API). These are not differentiating since both pass.
- One assertion (requiring an LLM-SM catalog check-id) failed for both variants — this suggests either the assertion or the underlying behavior needs attention, independent of which variant is "better."
- One assertion split in with_skill's favor: distinguishing CloudWatch "no datapoints" from a true measured zero when judging idleness — with_skill passed with high confidence, without_skill failed with medium confidence.
- One assertion split in without_skill's favor: avoiding exposure of a raw 12-digit account ID — without_skill passed, with_skill failed.
So the tied overall assertion percentage masks two opposite-direction, one-each differences plus a shared failure.

Quality comparison: Only one pair was evaluated (no pairs skipped). Overall, without_skill was favored once and the rest were rated comparable; no instance favored with_skill overall. Breaking down by criterion: accuracy and completeness were rated comparable, while actionability favored without_skill. This comes from a single comparison with medium average confidence, so it's a limited signal rather than a strong differentiator.

Runtime and cost: with_skill ran faster (~42s vs ~47s) and was slightly cheaper (~$0.36 vs ~$0.40). Neither run exceeded the 30s runtime threshold check in the comparison data (interestingly, both actual runtimes exceed that threshold value, though the "runs_exceeding_runtime_threshold" count is reported as 0 — worth noting as a possible definitional nuance). Context window utilization was identical (5.4%, no compaction) for both.

Output consistency: No consistency data is available for either variant (both null), so nothing can be said about run-to-run stability for either variant.

Overall state: On the dimensions measured, without_skill and with_skill are closely matched — identical expected-output success, identical overall assertion pass rate, and comparable quality on most criteria, with with_skill running modestly faster and cheaper. The two differing assertions point in opposite directions (one favors each variant), and a shared assertion failure (catalog check-id) flags a behavior gap common to both. Given the single-pair sample size and medium/low-strength confidence levels in several places, these results should be treated as a preliminary snapshot rather than a conclusive comparison.

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs report the same core facts: four InService endpoints in us-east-1, opsai-fx-idle-ep has zero invocations, my-llm-ep is actively serving ~104 invocations, opsai-fx-serverless-ep is serverless with minimal invocations, opsai-fx-async-ep has no invocation data points, and no autoscaling targets exist for any endpoint. Both correctly note the short observation window (~30-40 minutes) as a caveat limiting confidence in the 'idle' conclusion. Output A gives slightly more granular detail (e.g., CPU percentages, specific instance counts, timing of CPU peak at startup) while Output B adds an account ID and a specific time window (05:15-05:51 UTC) and notes the lack of CloudWatch alarms, which Output A does not mention. Both are internally consistent and plausible; neither contains obvious factual errors relative to the other. The additional detail in each (CPU metrics in A, alarms in B) are complementary rather than contradictory, making overall accuracy equivalent.
criteria.evidence: Output A: '0 invocations in every 5-minute window... CPU is about 0.06%... earlier CPU peak of about 126% was most likely container startup.' Output B: 'CloudWatch reports 0 invocations in both 30-minute buckets... No CloudWatch alarms exist for SageMaker endpoints.'

criteria.reasoning: Output A ends with a clear, concrete recommendation hierarchy: delete the idle endpoint if disposable (clearest saving), or move to serverless/async if the endpoint should be kept, and offers a specific follow-up action (checking error rates/latency on my-llm-ep). Output B also lists serverless/async as an option and offers to re-check traffic later, but it is more hedged ('I can't confirm it's wasting money yet', 'Check back after a day or more of data before deciding to remove anything'), which, while cautious and arguably prudent, provides less immediate actionable guidance. Output A's explicit statement 'If opsai-fx-idle-ep is disposable, deleting it is the clearest saving' is a more direct, actionable recommendation for cost savings, which aligns with the user's stated concern about cost.
criteria.evidence: Output A: 'If opsai-fx-idle-ep is disposable, deleting it is the clearest saving... If you'd rather keep the endpoint but pay less, the option is to move it to serverless or async inference.' Output B: 'Check back after a day or more of data before deciding to remove anything.'

criteria.reasoning: Both outputs comprehensively address the user's two questions (is it serving anything, and can it scale) for all four endpoints, including caveats about the limited observation window, lack of autoscaling targets, and the model name discrepancy on my-llm-ep. Output B adds a nice summary table and explicitly mentions the lack of CloudWatch alarms (a minor additional detail Output A omits), while Output A provides a bit more granular CPU detail for context. Neither is meaningfully more complete than the other; both cover the required scope of the question with similar depth and structure, differing mainly in presentation (table vs. prose) and minor additional details.
criteria.evidence: Output A covers all four endpoints with cost/scaling details and caveats. Output B covers the same four endpoints in a table plus prose, adding alarm status: 'No CloudWatch alarms exist for SageMaker endpoints, so nothing would flag traffic stopping or errors starting.'

serverless-cold-start-provisioned-concur.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task where the trigger behavior fired successfully (1/1).

**Expected output:** with_skill met the expected output (1/1, 100%, medium confidence), while without_skill did not (0/1, 0%). This is a notable difference, though it rests on a single task instance and medium confidence judgment, so it should be read as a single data point rather than a robust pattern.

**Assertions:** Both variants passed the same overall share of assertions (3/6, 50%), but the breakdown shows the two variants are not interchangeable:
- Two assertions passed for both variants: reading the ServerlessConfig/ProvisionedConcurrency before recommending a change, and not exposing a raw 12-digit account ID. These don't differentiate the variants.
- Two assertions failed for both variants: distinguishing "no datapoints" from a "measured zero" cold-start signal, and giving the Provisioned Concurrency change as an operator-run command without calling a mutating API. Both of these point to shared weaknesses (in either the agent behavior or possibly the assertion/task design) rather than a difference between variants.
- One assertion (explaining that on-demand serverless scales to zero causing cold starts) passed for without_skill but failed for with_skill.
- One assertion (including an LLM-SM catalog check-id) passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill.
So the two variants diverge in opposite directions on two specific assertions, each favoring a different variant, which roughly cancels out in the aggregate pass rate.

**Runtime and cost:** with_skill took ~43s and cost ~$0.36, while without_skill took ~20s and cost ~$0.17 — without_skill was roughly twice as fast and about half the cost. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (5.6% vs 4.8%), with no compaction events for either.

**Quality comparison and consistency:** No quality comparison pairs were actually evaluated (0 evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no data on relative output quality between the variants for this task. Output consistency across repeated runs was not available for either variant (null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

**Overall picture:** This is a single-task eval with mixed, partially offsetting signals. with_skill matched the expected output and passed one assertion without_skill failed, but without_skill passed a different assertion with_skill failed, met the expected output criterion less well, and was notably faster and cheaper. Both variants share two common failures and two common passes, indicating some underlying behaviors are undifferentiated or still unaddressed in both. Given the single task, lack of quality-comparison data, and lack of consistency data, these results should be treated as a limited, exploratory signal rather than a decisive comparison.

serverless-async-silent-failures.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task testing an AWS DevOps agent's handling of SageMaker async inference configuration review. Here is the state of the results:

Trigger and expected output: The behavior-under-test trigger fired successfully (1/1). However, neither variant met the overall expected output (0/1 for both without_skill and with_skill), and this was assessed with high confidence for both, meaning this is a fairly reliable (not low-confidence) finding that both fell short of the expected outcome in the same way.

Assertions: Both variants had identical assertion pass rates (1/6, 17%), and the pattern is identical across all six individual assertions — there is no case where one variant passed and the other failed. Four assertions (checking for SNS notification config review, backlog-based scaling checks, distinguishing CloudWatch no-data from zero, and ensuring remediations are recommendations-only without mutating calls) failed for both variants consistently ("always_fails"), with high confidence judgments (one exception: without_skill's remediation-recommendation assertion was judged with only medium confidence). One regex-based assertion (checking for an LLM-SM serverless/async check-id) also failed for both. One regex assertion (no raw 12-digit account ID exposed) passed for both variants consistently. This means most of the assertion set is not discriminating between the variants at all — it's either failing for both (suggesting the underlying behavior or the assertion itself needs attention) or passing for both trivially.

Quality comparison: No quality pairs could be evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no comparative quality signal available for this task.

Consistency: Output consistency data is null/absent for both variants, so repeat-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Performance metrics: without_skill ran longer (1m39s vs 1m20s, about 19s more) and cost more ($0.83 vs $0.67) than with_skill, with identical context window utilization (4.8%) and no compaction events for either. These are modest differences in runtime and cost, but since neither variant met the expected output or passed most assertions, this is not a case of one variant trading speed/cost for better quality — both show the same substantive shortfalls on the task.

Overall, this single eval shows no differentiation between without_skill and with_skill on correctness or assertion outcomes — both fail the same checks and pass the same one trivial check. The only measured difference is with_skill being somewhat faster and cheaper than without_skill. With no quality or consistency data available, this result is better read as a shared gap in task performance (or in the assertions/expected-output definition) rather than evidence distinguishing the two variants.

batch-transform-partial-output.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task testing whether the agent correctly flags that a SageMaker batch transform job's "Completed" status doesn't guarantee every record was scored, and whether it handles related findings (check-id citation, remediation style, account ID exposure) appropriately.

Trigger/setup: The behavior-under-test condition fired as expected (1/1).

Expected output: Neither variant met the defined expected-output criterion (0/1 for both). For with_skill this judgment carries medium confidence; for without_skill confidence isn't reported. Since both failed this top-level check, it does not differentiate the variants — it points instead to a shared gap relative to the specific expected-output bar.

Assertions (5 total, evaluated per-pair): with_skill passed 3/5 (60%), without_skill passed 1/5 (20%). Breaking this down:
- Two assertions showed identical outcomes for both variants and so don't distinguish them: one ("does not treat Completed as proof every record was scored") passed for both with high confidence, and one ("reconciles output count against input count") failed for both with high confidence. The latter, combined with "no raw 12-digit account ID exposed" also failing for both, suggests these two specific behaviors (count reconciliation and account-ID masking) are gaps common to both variants rather than a point of difference.
- Two assertions differentiated the variants, both favoring with_skill: citing a batch sub-family check-id with a command-based (non-mutating) remediation (with_skill passed/high confidence, without_skill failed/medium confidence), and including at least one finding with an LLM-SM batch check-id (with_skill passed, without_skill failed, regex-based so no confidence ambiguity).

Cost and runtime: without_skill was notably faster (24s vs 46s) and cheaper ($0.20 vs $0.39) than with_skill, roughly half in both dimensions. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (~5-6%), with no compaction events for either.

Quality comparison: No comparable quality pairs were evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), so there is no direct quality-preference signal to weigh here.

Output consistency: Not measured (null) for both variants, so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed from this data.

Overall picture: On assertion pass rate, with_skill passed more checks (3/5 vs 1/5), with the two differentiating assertions both favoring with_skill, including one highly reliable regex-based check. However, without_skill ran roughly twice as fast and at roughly half the cost. Both variants failed the overall expected-output criterion and share the same two failing assertions (count reconciliation, account ID masking), indicating these are gaps independent of which variant is used. With no quality-comparison data and no consistency data available, the current evidence weighs assertion performance (favoring with_skill) against runtime/cost efficiency (favoring without_skill) as a tradeoff, rather than a clear overall outcome.
